name: Passed pawns
goal: You can make a passed pawn from a pawn majority, use an outside or a protected passed pawn, stop an enemy passed pawn, and count the square of a pawn to see who wins a race.
intro: A passed pawn is a pawn with no enemy pawn in front of it, on its own file or on the files next to it, so only pieces can stop it. In an endgame it is often the strongest thing on the board, because the enemy king has to drop everything to stop it. Here you make one from a pawn majority (more pawns than your opponent on one side of the board), use an outside passed pawn, one far from all the other pawns, to pull the enemy king away, and use a protected passed pawn, one guarded by another pawn, which the enemy king can never take. You also stop an enemy passed pawn by putting your king in its path, and use the square of the pawn to tell whether a king is still in time to catch it.

parts.title: Two against one
parts.keyIdea: Two pawns against one can make a passed pawn: push the one with no enemy pawn in front of it.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. On the queenside you have two pawns, on a4 and b5, against Black's one on b6: a pawn majority. Black's king is heading over, so there is no time to lose.

notes.text: 39.a5 pushes the pawn that has no black pawn in front of it. If 39...bxa5, then 40.b6, and your b-pawn is passed and too fast for Black's king.
Black's king is going for b5, so 40.a6 runs with the a-pawn. Nothing stands between it and a8.
Black's king took the b5 pawn, but that was far too slow: after 41.a7 the pawn promotes next move, and the king cannot reach a8 in time.

parts.title: The outside passed pawn
parts.keyIdea: An outside passed pawn keeps the enemy king busy at the edge; while it is there, your king wins pawns elsewhere.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are Black. Your h-pawn is passed, and it stands on the other side of the board from all the other pawns: an outside passed pawn. White's king on g4 has to watch it, which keeps that king a long way from White's pawns on b4 and d4.
parts.line: h3 Kxh3 Kf5 Kg3 Ke4 b5 Kxd4

notes.text: 45...h3 gives the pawn up on purpose. To stop it, White's king has to chase it towards the corner, even further from the centre.
While White's king took the pawn, 46...Kf5 sets off for the centre and the d4 pawn.
47...Ke4 puts your king next to the d4 pawn, and White's king is too far away to defend it.

48...Kxd4 wins the d4 pawn. Your d-pawn is now a passed pawn with your king just in front of it to lead the way, and White's king is stuck on the far side of the board, so the d-pawn will decide the game.

parts.title: A pawn that guards a pawn
parts.keyIdea: A passed pawn guarded by another pawn holds the enemy king back on its own, so your king is free to win pawns elsewhere.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Your pawn on e5 is a passed pawn, and the pawn on f4 guards it: a protected passed pawn. Black's king cannot take it, and it cannot wander far from it either, or the pawn runs. Your own king is free to go after Black's pawns.

notes.text: 51.Kg4 goes after the pawn on h4, and it is the only move that wins. Black's king has to stay near your e-pawn, so it cannot come over to help.

Black tried 51...g5, giving up a pawn to break up yours. 52.fxg5 takes it. The e-pawn is no longer guarded, but now your g-pawn is a passed pawn too. If Black's king takes the e-pawn, yours takes the h4 pawn and walks the g-pawn up the board.
Black pushed 52...h3, and 53.Kxh3 takes it. Black has no pawns left, and you have two passed pawns: Black's king cannot stop both of them.

parts.title: A pawn two steps from promoting
parts.keyIdea: Stop a passed pawn by putting your king on its path; then your own passed pawn can pull the enemy king away.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Black's d-pawn is a passed pawn two steps from promoting, with Black's king close by. Your king has to get in front of it, and only one route works.
parts.line: Ke1 Kd4 Kd2 Ke4 h4 Kd4 h5 Ke5 Kxd3

notes.text: 55.Ke1 heads for d1 and d2, the squares in front of the pawn. 55.Ke3 looks closer, but after 55...Kc3 Black's king supports the pawn all the way to d1, and it promotes.
56.Kd2: your king stands right in front of the pawn, so the pawn cannot move.
57.h4: now your own passed pawn sets off. Black's king cannot guard the d3 pawn and stop this one for long.
58.h5 pushes on. If Black's king stays near the d3 pawn, the h-pawn runs through and promotes.
Black's king went after the h-pawn, so 59.Kxd3 takes the d3 pawn. Next your king heads for the a5 pawn, and Black's king, busy on the kingside, is too far away to save it.

parts.title: Two passed pawns, two squares
parts.keyIdea: When both sides have a passed pawn, count both squares: a king inside the square of a pawn can still catch it, a king outside cannot.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Each side has one passed pawn: yours on g4, Black's on b3. Black's pawn needs two moves to promote and yours needs four, so do not start the race yet. Picture the square of each pawn: a square with one side running from the pawn to the square where it promotes.
parts.line: Kc3 Ka4 Kb2 Kb5 g5 Kc4 g6 Kd5 g7

notes.text: 62.Kc3 steps into the square of Black's pawn, the square with corners b3, b1, d1 and d3, and it is the only move that wins. From d4 your king was just outside it: after 62.g5, Black's pawn would run to b2 and b1 and promote long before yours.
Black's king came to a4 to protect the pawn, so you cannot take it. 63.Kb2 blocks it instead: your king stands right in front of the pawn, and it cannot move any more.
Black's king set off for your g-pawn, but it is too late. On b5 it is outside the square of your pawn, the square with corners g4, g8, c8 and c4, so 64.g5 starts the race.
The square gets smaller with every step the pawn takes, and Black's king on c4 is still outside it. 65.g6.
66.g7: the pawn promotes next move, and Black's king on d5 is far away. Black's b-pawn cannot move either, because your king stands in front of it.
